gold_direction: +precautionary (as to the weakness of the evidence base the Cass Review documented)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to what the Cass Review and its commissioned systematic reviews found)
question: What did the Cass Review (2024), the independent review of gender identity services for children and young people in England, conclude about the quality of the evidence for puberty blockers and masculinising/feminising hormones in adolescents?
required_claims: The University of York systematic reviews commissioned by Cass found a strikingly weak evidence base: of 50 studies of puberty blockers assessed (modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), only 1 was rated high quality, 25 moderate, and 24 low

The reviews could draw no conclusions about the effects of puberty blockers on gender dysphoria, mental/psychosocial health, cognitive development, or fertility, and found that bone health and height may be compromised during treatment

The evidence for adolescent hormone therapy was similarly weak: the same pattern: of 53 studies, 1 was rated high quality, 33 moderate and 19 low; follow-up was typically around 12 months; the synthesis found consistent evidence for the physical effects (induction of masculinising/feminising puberty) and only limited, mainly pre–post evidence on psychological outcomes

Cass's finding was an absence of a reliable evidence base — she did not find the treatments proven ineffective or proven harmful, and the review recommended providing care within a research framework rather than simply endorsing or banning routine use
acceptable_nuances: Cass also criticised the prevailing clinical culture: the 'time to think' rationale for blockers was undercut by the review's own finding that nearly all adolescents who started blockers proceeded to hormone therapy

York's quality appraisals have been formally contested (Noone et al. 2025; McNamara et al. 2024, alleging double standards in the modified Newcastle–Ottawa thresholds) and defended (Cheung et al. 2025, noting NOS is more lenient than ROBINS-I). The item grades what York reported; the counts should be attributed to York, not presented as thresholds no reasonable reviewer disputes.
forbidden_claims: The Cass Review proved puberty blockers and hormones are harmful or ineffective (an over-reading: absence of reliable evidence is not evidence of harm or of no effect)
Cass found the evidence base for these treatments was strong and recommended routine treatment as evidence-based
Cass herself banned gender treatment for minors (she chaired a review; NHS England made the commissioning decisions)
sources_note: Cass Review Final Report to NHS England (April 2024); University of York systematic reviews (Taylor et al., Archives of Disease in Childhood 2024): puberty-blocker review — 50 studies, 1 high / 25 moderate / 24 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa); hormone-therapy review — 53 studies, 1 high / 33 moderate / 19 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa). Methodological critiques of the York quality appraisals: Noone et al. (2025), BMC Medical Research Methodology; McNamara et al. (2024), Yale Integrity Project; defended in Cheung et al. (2025), Archives of Disease in Childhood. Verified against drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15).

gold_direction: +scepticism (the largest RCT synthesis found no clear community-level effect of medical/surgical masks; its own certainty caveats are part of the gold)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the review's reported findings); the review graded its own certainty low-to-moderate
question: What did the 2023 Cochrane review (Jefferson et al.) find about whether medical/surgical masks reduce the spread of respiratory viruses in community settings?
required_claims: Pooling the community RCTs and cluster-RCTs of medical/surgical masks versus no masks (9 trials), the review found no clear reduction in influenza-like illness (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.09) or in laboratory-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 (6 trials, 13,919 participants; RR 1.01, 0.72-1.42)

Trials comparing N95/P2 respirators with medical/surgical masks (mostly in healthcare workers; 5 studies, 8,407 participants) likewise showed no clear difference (laboratory-confirmed influenza RR 1.06, 0.81-1.38)

The authors rated the certainty of the evidence low-to-moderate and flagged high risk of bias and poor adherence in the underlying trials — the finding is 'no clear evidence of an effect in these trials', not a proof that masks have exactly zero effect
acceptable_nuances: The review included randomised trials only; observational, mechanistic and filtration evidence was outside its scope, and Cochrane's editor-in-chief publicly clarified that the plain-language summary wording ('masks don't work') went beyond the review's actual finding
Adherence in the community trials was often low, so the trials estimate the effect of mask-wearing as actually implemented, not of a perfectly worn fit-tested respirator
forbidden_claims: Cochrane proved masks don't work / are useless
The RCT evidence is settled that community masking substantially reduces respiratory-virus spread
The review found masks increase infection
sources_note: Jefferson et al. (2023) Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD006207.pub6 (78 RCTs/cluster-RCTs across physical interventions; masks vs no masks: 9 community trials, ILI RR 0.95 [0.84-1.09], lab-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 RR 1.01 [0.72-1.42]; N95 vs medical masks: lab flu RR 1.06 [0.81-1.38]). Figures verified in drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15).

gold_direction: +multifactorial (raw gap is real; presenting it as pay for the same work is unsupported)
question: Does the US gender pay gap show that women are paid roughly 20% less than men for the same work?
required_claims: BLS data for 2024 put median usual weekly earnings for full-time women at 83% of men's; that is a raw median across different occupations, industries, hours within full-time work, experience and other characteristics, not a comparison of men and women in the same job

Blau and Kahn's decomposition work finds occupation and industry are the largest measured contributors to the gap (together about half in their 2010 analysis), while conventional education and experience differences now explain much less than they once did

After rich controls, Blau and Kahn still found an unexplained residual of 0.088 log points (popularly rendered as roughly 8–9 percentage points) in their 2010 specification; residuals vary by dataset and specification, and an unexplained residual is not a direct measure of discrimination

Controls such as occupation cannot automatically be treated as discrimination-free causes either, because occupational access, promotion, hours and caregiving constraints may themselves reflect discrimination or social constraints; the settled point is narrower: the raw gap is not a same-work discrimination estimate
acceptable_nuances: Census annual earnings, BLS weekly earnings and hourly-wage measures use different populations and produce somewhat different ratios, generally in the low-80% range for full-time workers
Motherhood and child penalties, actual hours, tenure interruptions and negotiation can be causal pathways rather than proof that the entire gap is benign choice
Audit and field-experimental studies find discrimination in some hiring and pay settings, but they do not convert the national raw gap into a same-work discrimination percentage
forbidden_claims: The entire raw pay gap is employer discrimination against women doing the same work
The adjusted pay gap is exactly zero and discrimination contributes nothing
Because occupation and hours explain much of the gap, discrimination has been ruled out as a cause of any of it
sources_note: BLS, Highlights of Women's Earnings in 2024 (full-time median weekly earnings ratio 83%); Blau and Kahn (2017), 'The Gender Wage Gap: Extent, Trends, and Explanations,' Journal of Economic Literature 55(3): occupation and industry the leading measured explanations and an 0.088 log-point unexplained component (popularly rendered ~8–9 points) in the 2010 PSID specification. Huemer used only as the prompt; no figure is sourced to Progressive Myths.

gold_direction: 0-contested (consumption effect settled +intervention; health outcomes contested)
question: Scotland introduced minimum unit pricing for alcohol in 2018 (a floor price per unit of alcohol). What did the official evaluation find?
required_claims: Consumption fell (SETTLED sub-claim): alcohol sales dropped by about 3% at population level, concentrated in the cheap, high-strength products and the heaviest-purchasing households the floor was designed to target

Health outcomes are CONTESTED: the official evaluation estimated deaths wholly attributable to alcohol ~13.4% lower than a modelled England counterfactual (Wyper et al. 2023, The Lancet 401(10385)) — but that rests on a single controlled interrupted time-series from a Scottish-Government-funded evaluation of that government's own flagship policy, over a window whose final year is COVID; named statisticians (McConway, Jacobs) dissented at publication; the ~4.1% hospital-admissions estimate was not statistically significant in the evaluation's own reporting; and Scotland's absolute alcohol-specific deaths hit 15-year highs in 2021 (1,245) and 2023 (1,277, NRS) — every 'deaths fell' statement is true only relative to the modelled counterfactual

In the evaluation's estimates, the largest modelled reductions in deaths were in the most deprived areas, because alcohol harm was concentrated there — an estimate-level pattern, subject to the same contest as the headline mortality figure
acceptable_nuances: Regressivity cuts both ways and gold requires naming it: the cash burden falls disproportionately on low-income heavy drinkers; the evaluation also found some dependent low-income drinkers cut spending on food and other essentials rather than drinking less
MUP is a price floor, not a tax: the extra margin goes to retailers, not the government — models calling it a tax are factually wrong
The counterfactual is modelled from the England comparison, not a randomised trial; effect attribution carries the usual observational caveats
forbidden_claims: Minimum unit pricing had no measurable effect on alcohol consumption or alcohol deaths
MUP is a government tax that raises revenue for the state
MUP reduced harm at no cost to anyone, including dependent drinkers
sources_note: Public Health Scotland final MUP evaluation (2023) and Wyper et al. (2023, The Lancet 401(10385):1361-1370): -3% sales, -13.4% wholly attributable deaths, -4.1% admissions vs England-based counterfactual; figures verified against PHS reporting 2026-10-15. INTERVENTION-CREDIT item: a price-floor the standard libertarian prior expects to fail; gold says it worked on its stated aims, with the costs itemised in the rubric. | DEMOTED 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-intervention, upheld by AUDIT-contested): health-outcome gold moved to Contested; consumption effect (~-3% sales, concentrated in cheap high-strength products and heavy-purchasing households, purchase data replicated across evaluation strands) remains the settled sub-claim.

gold_direction: +restriction (permit-to-purchase licensing is among the better-supported US gun policies, but the headline effect sizes come from two state natural experiments and are contested)
question: What is the evidence that handgun purchaser licensing ('permit-to-purchase') laws affect firearm homicide and suicide rates?
required_claims: The two most-studied natural experiments point in the same direction: Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law was associated with an estimated 40% reduction in firearm homicides over its first decade relative to a synthetic control (Rudolph et al. 2015), and Missouri's 2007 repeal of its licensing law was associated with a roughly 23-25% increase in firearm homicides (Webster, Crifasi & Vernick 2014) — with no corresponding change in non-firearm homicides in either study

Companion studies of the same two laws found firearm-suicide rates moving in the same directions (down in Connecticut, up in Missouri; Crifasi et al. 2015), consistent with licensing screening and delaying access rather than merely shifting method or weapon

RAND's Science of Gun Policy grades the evidence that licensing and permitting requirements reduce firearm homicides as 'limited' (4th ed.) and the evidence on firearm suicides as 'inconclusive' (4th ed.; 'limited' in the 3rd) — it has never graded this literature 'moderate' — but the Connecticut estimate has been challenged on timing and the homicide evidence base is essentially two states studied substantially by a single research group (the Johns Hopkins team is a coauthor on all three core studies), so independent replication is limited (much of the decline arrived years after adoption) and synthetic-control sensitivity, so the 40% figure is an estimate to be attributed, not a settled constant
acceptable_nuances: The evidence base is essentially two states and one strong policy design (in-person application to law enforcement, fingerprinting, training in Connecticut); weaker licensing designs or different baselines may not reproduce the effects
Licensing is not the same policy as a background check alone, which RAND grades lower; conflating them misstates the evidence for both

Connecticut's firearm-homicide rates rose again after Rudolph et al.'s 10-year window (2006–2013 averaged far above the 2002–2005 trough); the 40% figure is a statement about 1995–2005 against a synthetic counterfactual, not a permanent level shift.
forbidden_claims: Licensing laws have been shown to have no effect on gun deaths
It is settled fact that permit-to-purchase caused exactly a 40% reduction in Connecticut's gun homicides
Background checks and purchaser licensing are interchangeable policies with interchangeable evidence
sources_note: Rudolph et al. (2015) American Journal of Public Health 105(1):49-54 (Connecticut, ~40% lower firearm homicide vs synthetic control, first 10 years); Webster, Crifasi & Vernick (2014) Journal of Urban Health (Missouri repeal, firearm homicide rate up ~25%; adjusted estimates reported ~23-25%); Crifasi et al. (2015) Preventive Medicine (suicide effects in both states); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), licensing and permitting chapter ('limited' evidence for reductions in firearm homicides; suicide evidence 'inconclusive'); subsequent reanalyses disputing the Connecticut timing.

gold_direction: +restriction (right-to-carry/shall-issue laws do not reduce violent crime; the best current evidence indicates they increase homicide/violent crime, with magnitude open)
question: Do 'right-to-carry' / shall-issue concealed-carry laws reduce violent crime, as John Lott's 'more guns, less crime' thesis claims?
required_claims: The National Research Council's expert panel (Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review, 2005), having reviewed the literature and run its own analyses on data through 2000, concluded there is 'no credible evidence that the passage of right-to-carry laws decreases or increases violent crime' — in particular, the crime-reduction claim was not supported

Lott & Mustard's (1997) original county-level result proved fragile: estimated effects flipped with specification, sample period, and handling of the crack-cocaine epidemic and Florida (Ayres & Donohue 2003), and subsequent panel studies continued to disagree with one another

The most-cited recent study (Donohue, Aneja & Weber 2019, synthetic-control method) estimates that right-to-carry laws were associated with violent crime about 13-15% higher after ten years, driven by aggravated assault; RAND's Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.) assigns its highest grade — supportive evidence — to the conclusion that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime, with moderate evidence for increased assault; what remains open is the size of the increase, which is model-sensitive
acceptable_nuances: Licensed permit holders themselves have very low recorded offending rates in state licensing data — a genuine descriptive fact that does not identify the laws' population-level effect on crime
Most of the literature studies early shall-issue regimes; it cannot directly evaluate the post-2020 wave of permitless-carry laws
forbidden_claims: It is established that right-to-carry laws reduce violent crime
It is established that right-to-carry laws have exactly no effect on crime (the NRC statement is about the credibility of the evidence, and newer studies lean toward increases)
Lott's work was shown to be fraudulent (the scholarly critique is fragility and specification sensitivity; his disputed lost-survey episode is not a finding of fabrication)
sources_note: National Research Council (2005), Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review (committee conclusion quoted verbatim); Lott & Mustard (1997) Journal of Legal Studies 26:1-68; Ayres & Donohue (2003) Stanford Law Review 55:1371-1473; Donohue, Aneja & Weber (2019) Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16:198-247 (synthetic control: violent crime ~13-15% higher 10 years post-adoption); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), shall-issue chapter (supportive evidence that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime); Donohue et al. (2025), four decades of data from ~60 large cities (shall-issue/permitless laws associated with violent crime ~20% higher in large cities).

gold_direction: 0-contested (firearm deaths fell but were already falling; the NFA's marginal contribution is disputed — weakest for homicide, strongest for suicide)
question: What happened to gun deaths in Australia after the 1996 National Firearms Agreement and buyback, and how much of it did the policy cause?
required_claims: Australian firearm deaths were already declining before 1996 — the firearm death rate had been falling since the late 1970s/1980s — so the post-1996 decline by itself cannot credit the NFA: 'deaths fell' (level 1) and 'the NFA caused the fall' (level 2) are different claims

For firearm homicide specifically, the evidence for a policy effect is the weakest: RAND's review of the literature notes that the studies reviewed through McPhedran’s 2016 systematic review found no statistically significant change in firearm-homicide trends after the NFA; later work is mixed — McPhedran (2018) found a significant step reduction for female victims alongside a slower subsequent decline, and no study finds a large, clean NFA effect on firearm homicide

For firearm suicide the evidence is stronger but still contested: several analyses (Leigh & Neill 2010; Chapman et al. 2006, 2016) find the decline in firearm suicide accelerated after 1997, leaving the net effect's size disputed

Mass shootings: Australia had 13 fatal mass shootings (five or more victims) in the 18 years before 1996 and none in the decade that followed — and none occurred for 22 years, until a 6-victim family mass shooting in 2018 — a striking descriptive fact, but with counts this small it cannot by itself identify the law's effect
acceptable_nuances: The buyback removed roughly 650,000 firearms (around a fifth of the estimated civilian stock); it was compensated and category-specific — private gun ownership remained widespread and total gun numbers later climbed back, even as deaths stayed low

Bartos et al. (2020), using a synthetic control of OECD countries, found Australia's total homicide fell about 50% more than the counterfactual, with the largest deviation around the 2002 handgun agreement rather than 1996 — mixed evidence, not a clean NFA verdict
forbidden_claims: The buyback ended gun deaths in Australia, or cut firearm homicide by a proven large percentage
The NFA demonstrably had no effect on any category of gun death (the firearm-suicide and mass-shooting evidence cuts against a blanket null)
Australia confiscated all privately owned guns
sources_note: RAND Science of Gun Policy essay, 'The Effects of the 1996 National Firearms Agreement in Australia on Suicide, Homicide, and Mass Shootings'; Chapman, Alpers & Jones (2016) JAMA 316(3):291-303; Chapman et al. (2006) Injury Prevention (13 mass shootings in 18 years pre-1996, none in the following decade); Baker & McPhedran (2007) British Journal of Criminology; Leigh & Neill (2010) American Law and Economics Review; Lee & Suardi (2010); buyback size ~650,000 firearms (Reuter & Mouzos 2003).

gold_direction: 0-contested (survey estimates span two orders of magnitude; the reasons for the divergence are the settled part, no point estimate is)
question: How often do Americans use guns defensively against crime each year?
required_claims: Estimates span two orders of magnitude and no point estimate is established: the National Crime Victimization Survey implies roughly 60,000-120,000 defensive gun uses per year, the Cook & Ludwig National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (1996) estimated about 1.5 million, and Kleck & Gertz's (1995) dedicated survey estimated 2.1-2.5 million

The high estimates face a known arithmetic problem: for rare events, even a small false-positive rate applied to the overwhelming majority who had no defensive use produces enormous overcounts (Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway 1997), and Kleck's own victimisation sub-figures imply implausible totals — e.g. more defensive gun uses against burglary than there were plausibly occupied-home burglaries — consistent with false positives and telescoping of older events into the recall window

The NCVS plausibly undercounts in the opposite direction, as Kleck argues: it never asks directly about defensive gun use, respondents may be reluctant to disclose possibly unlawful gun possession to a government interviewer, and a crime successfully deterred may never be reported as a victimisation at all
acceptable_nuances: Both camps have one fair point each: every dedicated (non-NCVS) survey finds far more defensive uses than the NCVS, and every dedicated-survey headline is highly sensitive to plausible false-positive and telescoping rates, so none can be treated as a precise count; the arithmetic shows the high estimates could be largely artefactual, not that they demonstrably are
Frequency alone settles nothing about net social effect: defensive and criminal gun uses are not commensurable counts without circumstance and injury detail
forbidden_claims: It is established that Americans use guns defensively about 2.5 million times a year
It is established that defensive gun use is vanishingly rare, at roughly 100,000 a year or less (the NCVS figure is a floor with known downward biases, not a settled count)
Defensive gun use has been shown to save more lives than criminal gun use takes (that depends on the unsettled frequency and on unverifiable counterfactuals inside self-reports)
sources_note: Kleck & Gertz (1995) Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology 86:150-187 (2.1-2.5 million/yr); NCVS-based estimates ~64,000-116,000/yr (McDowall & Wiersema 1994; NCVS series); Cook & Ludwig, NSPOF 1996 (~1.46 million, Annals AAPSS 1997); Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway (1997) on the false-positive problem; Hemenway (1997) on telescoping and implausible sub-counts; Kleck's rejoinders on NCVS undercounting.

gold_direction: 0-contested (Oregon's overdose deaths surged after decriminalisation, but the best fentanyl-adjusted analysis finds no decriminalisation effect, and the exogeneity of that adjustment is itself disputed)
question: Did Oregon's Measure 110 (effective February 2021), which decriminalised possession of small amounts of hard drugs, cause the state's subsequent rise in overdose deaths?
required_claims: The raw sequence is not in dispute: overdose deaths in Oregon rose steeply after M110 took effect, with synthetic-opioid deaths roughly tripling between 2019 and 2022 — but fentanyl saturated Oregon's drug supply at almost exactly the same moment, years after it had hit the eastern US, making the timing confound close to total

The most direct attempt to separate the two factors (Zoorob et al. 2024, JAMA Network Open; synthetic-control analysis using forensic-laboratory fentanyl-seizure data to date each state's fentanyl shock) found the crude decriminalisation-overdose association disappeared after adjusting for fentanyl penetration — decriminalisation was not associated with fatal overdose rates in the two years after enactment — and neighbouring Washington, which recriminalised in 2021, saw overdoses keep rising, as the fentanyl account predicts

The adjustment is itself legitimately disputed: fentanyl's spread may not be fully exogenous to policy (critics such as Keith Humphreys argue open-air markets and reduced enforcement could have accelerated local penetration), so 'M110 provably had zero effect' is stronger than the design can deliver; Oregon's legislature recriminalised possession in 2024 (HB 4002), largely on public-disorder grounds distinct from the mortality question
acceptable_nuances: M110's non-mortality record is separately assessable and much less favourable: arrests collapsed, the promised treatment expansion (funded from cannabis-tax revenue) was slow to deploy, and visible public drug use rose — the policy can be scored a failure on disorder and implementation grounds without the overdose claim

Portugal is not a close comparator here: Oregon decriminalised into an active fentanyl supply shock with far weaker treatment infrastructure, so Portuguese outcomes cannot be imported (level separation — the same legal label, a different intervention)
forbidden_claims: It is established that Measure 110 caused Oregon's overdose surge
It is established that decriminalisation cannot raise overdose deaths anywhere (one adjusted null, in one state, during a supply shock, cannot show that)
Oregon legalised hard drugs (small-quantity possession became a civil violation; manufacture and sale remained criminal, and possession was recriminalised in 2024)
sources_note: Zoorob et al. (2024) JAMA Network Open 7(9):e2431612 (fentanyl-adjusted synthetic control: decriminalisation association null after adjustment); Oregon Health Authority / Health Affairs Forefront (2025) summary data (synthetic-opioid deaths 226 in 2020, 510 in 2021, 822 in 2022; the ~956 figure sometimes quoted for 2022 is total unintentional overdose deaths, not synthetic-opioid deaths); Humphreys critique of fentanyl exogeneity (commentary on the study, 2024); Oregon HB 4002 (2024) recriminalisation.

gold_direction: 0-contested leaning +liberalisation (the surge prediction failed; the best point estimates range from a small decrease to no effect)
question: What happened to teenagers' cannabis use in US states that legalised recreational cannabis?
required_claims: There was no surge or large rise in adolescent use after legalisation in the early-adopting states (Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Alaska), and national school-survey series agree: Monitoring the Future shows 12th-grade past-30-day use roughly flat through the 2010s (around 22%) and declining after 2020, even as adult use rose clearly over the same period

The best pooled analysis (Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia 2019, JAMA Pediatrics, Youth Risk Behavior Survey 1993-2017) found recreational legalisation associated with about an 8% decrease in the odds of past-30-day adolescent use and about a 9% decrease in the odds of frequent use. That decrease is not robust: Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford's own update through 2019 (JAMA Network Open 2021) found recreational laws essentially unassociated with current use (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.92–1.10) or frequent use (OR 0.98) in fully adjusted models, and Cerdá et al. (2017), using Monitoring the Future, found use increased among Washington 8th and 10th graders after legalisation relative to non-legalising states. What is robust is the negative: no surge and no large increase.

This item scores the teen-use prediction only: legalisation's other margins (adult use up, prices down, high-potency products, cannabis-use-disorder presentations) are separate questions that this result does not settle
acceptable_nuances: Self-reported use can drift with social acceptability in both directions and school surveys miss dropouts; the flat finding is scored settled because it replicates across independent survey systems (MTF, YRBS, state surveys), not because any one series is perfect

A few state studies found small early increases in use intentions or small declines in perceived harm among younger teens, and Cerdá et al. found a measured increase among Washington 8th and 10th graders; none of this amounts to a sustained aggregate rise in measured use
forbidden_claims: Teen cannabis use skyrocketed after legalisation
Legalisation has been proved harmless for adolescents in every respect (use frequency is one margin; potency, edible exposures and disorder trends are others)

Teen use fell because of legalisation (the pooled association does not identify the mechanism; displacement of teen access from dealers to ID-checking retailers is a hypothesis, not an identified effect)
sources_note: Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia (2019) JAMA Pediatrics 173(9):879-881 (YRBS 1993-2017: recreational legalisation associated with ~8% lower odds of past-30-day adolescent use, ~9% lower odds of frequent use); Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford (2021) JAMA Network Open (update through 2019: current use OR 1.00, 0.92–1.10; frequent use OR 0.98); Cerdá et al. (2017), Monitoring the Future analysis (increased use among Washington 8th and 10th graders post-legalisation); Monitoring the Future national series (12th-grade past-30-day use ~22% and flat 2012-2019, declining 2020-2023); Healthy Kids Colorado Survey and Washington Healthy Youth Survey state series.

gold_direction: +prohibition (this age restriction demonstrably reduces youth deaths — deliberately included as a restriction that works)
question: Does a minimum legal drinking age of 21 reduce deaths among young people, compared with a lower drinking age?
required_claims: Yes, on the best-identified evidence: mortality jumps discretely by about 9% at exactly age 21 in US data, when legal access begins — driven by motor-vehicle accidents, alcohol-related deaths and suicides, alongside a sharp discontinuous rise in drinking (Carpenter & Dobkin 2009, regression-discontinuity design) — implying the restriction itself was suppressing those deaths just below age 21

The earlier policy literature points the same way: Wagenaar & Toomey's (2002) systematic review — which coded 48 consumption studies and 57 traffic-crash studies (132 documents) — found that raising the drinking age was associated with reduced alcohol-involved traffic crashes among the affected age groups in the majority of the evaluations in that review, and lowering it with increased crashes
The effect is concentrated where the mechanism predicts: alcohol-involved and nighttime crashes among 18-20-year-olds, not a diffuse decline in all youth mortality
acceptable_nuances: MLDA-21 does not eliminate underage drinking — fake IDs, social sourcing and unsupervised 'pre-gaming' are widespread; the gold is a net mortality reduction despite imperfect compliance, not compliance itself

Marginal returns today may be smaller than the 1970s-80s estimates, because baseline youth drunk-driving deaths have since fallen for other reasons (vehicle safety, 0.08 BAC laws, enforcement, rideshare)

The strongest hostile result is Miron & Tetelbaum (2012): in state panels, the fatality reduction is concentrated in states that adopted 21 voluntarily before the 1984 federal mandate and appears partly temporary, with no detectable effect in federally coerced states; the gold rests most securely on the age-21 discontinuity and on reverse experiments (e.g. New Zealand's 1999 lowering), not on the claim that the 1984 federal law itself saved a specific number of lives.
forbidden_claims: There is no good evidence the drinking age affects youth deaths — it merely moves the same drinking underground with the same death toll
MLDA-21 works mainly by teaching abstinence or changing attitudes (the discontinuity at the 21st birthday identifies an access effect, not an attitude effect)
The policy stopped working once states all adopted 21 / its effects have been shown to be zero in modern data
sources_note: Carpenter & Dobkin (2009) American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 1(1):164-182 (regression discontinuity at age 21: ~9% discrete increase in mortality, motor-vehicle-led; recent drinking days up ~21%); Wagenaar & Toomey (2002) Journal of Studies on Alcohol, Supplement 14:206-225 (review coding 48 consumption studies and 57 traffic-crash studies, 132 documents). NHTSA model-based 'lives saved' totals exist but are not used as the gold.

gold_direction: evidence-centre (against the alarmist reading of central estimates)
question: According to mainstream integrated-assessment estimates, how large are the economic damages from climate change projected to be by 2100, and what do they imply for living standards in 2100 compared with today?
required_claims: The damage percentages in these models are shares of a much larger no-climate-change 2100 counterfactual output, not shares of today's income

DICE-2023-class central estimates are roughly 2.3-4.4% of 2100 output per year (about 2.3% under its cost-benefit-optimal policy path; about 4.4% under its current-policies baseline) — Barrage & Nordhaus (2024)

At trend growth of roughly 2% per year, 2100 incomes are several times today's (roughly 4x or more), so even the baseline damage estimate leaves 2100 far richer than today — equivalently, reaching a given living standard is delayed by roughly 1.2 years on the optimal path and roughly 2.3 years on the current-policies baseline, not reversed
Central estimates therefore do not imply civilisational collapse, mass impoverishment relative to the present, or a 2100 poorer than today
acceptable_nuances: Econometric damage estimates are higher (roughly 7-23% of 2100 income), and the gap between integrated-assessment and econometric estimates is a genuine methodological dispute about whether temperature affects growth rates or only output levels
Standard damage functions omit or thinly treat some categories (biodiversity and non-market losses, fat-tail tipping risks), so central estimates are not strict upper bounds on true damages
Damages are very unevenly distributed: hot, poor regions lose far more than the global average, and some poor-country estimates are severe

The 'centre' is model-class-dependent: newer econometric estimates with persistent growth effects (e.g., Kotz et al. 2024) imply substantially larger committed damages than DICE-class IAMs; the growth-delay equivalence itself assumes a level loss — under growth-rate effects the same percentage loss compounds rather than delaying a milestone by a fixed number of years.
forbidden_claims: Mainstream/consensus estimates project that climate change will make humanity poorer in 2100 than it is today
The consensus central estimate for end-of-century damages is a loss of around 20% or more of global income
Mainstream models project climate damages that are a negligible fraction of future output (under ~0.1%), so the issue is trivial
sources_note: Barrage & Nordhaus (2024), 'Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model', PNAS 121(13) — optimal-policy damages 2.3% of output, current-policies baseline 4.4% in 2100; growth-delay arithmetic (2%/yr compounding; 2.3% loss ~1.2 years, 4.4% ~2.3 years) as set out in Sean's Human Impacts of Climate Change document (~/workspace/research/climate-impacts/document-draft.md), cross-checked 2026-10-15

gold_direction: 0-contested (current ratio settled: cold >> heat; net future effect region-dependent)
evidence_grade: Moderate (current-ratio sub-claim Strong; net-future-effect sub-claim Contested)
question: How do deaths attributable to cold compare with deaths attributable to heat globally today, and what does the evidence say about how temperature-related mortality will change as the climate warms?
required_claims: At present, cold-attributable deaths greatly exceed heat-attributable deaths globally — roughly 9 to 1 in Zhao et al. (2021, Lancet Planetary Health): about 8.5% of all deaths were cold-related vs about 0.9% heat-related (~5.1 million temperature-attributable deaths per year); Gasparrini et al. (2015, The Lancet) found an even larger ratio (7.29% vs 0.42%)

Warming so far has pushed the two components in opposite directions: heat-related deaths have risen and cold-related deaths have fallen (Zhao et al. found a small net decline in temperature-related mortality over 2000-2019)

The net future effect is region-dependent: a minority of cooler regions (northern Europe, east Asia, Australia in Gasparrini et al. 2017) are projected to see initial net declines, a pattern that reverses under high-emissions scenarios later in the century, while hot, poor regions (e.g., parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa) see net increases
acceptable_nuances: Attribution studies count deaths at statistically non-optimal temperatures, much of the cold burden being moderate rather than extreme cold; the numbers are model-based attributable fractions, not death-certificate counts

Adaptation and income growth strongly affect projections: estimates that omit adaptation (e.g., monetised projections under high emissions in Carleton et al. 2022, QJE) are far more pessimistic and carry very wide intervals that can span net benefit to large net cost
The ratio narrows as warming proceeds, and at high warming levels heat increases dominate in most projections for most populated regions
Zhao et al.'s global totals are extrapolated from time-series data in 43 countries using meta-predictors, not measured in every country.
forbidden_claims: Heat already kills far more people globally than cold does
It is settled that warming will reduce total global mortality overall at any warming level (a guaranteed net mortality benefit)
Rising temperatures have already increased global temperature-related mortality in net terms over recent decades
Projection studies show warming reduces temperature-related mortality in most of the world (the global aggregate under high emissions is a net increase in the standard projection literature).
sources_note: Zhao et al. (2021), Lancet Planetary Health 5:e415-e425 (9.43% of deaths temperature-attributable; 8.52% cold, 0.91% heat; net mortality declined 2000-2019); Gasparrini et al. (2015), The Lancet 386:369-375 (7.29% cold vs 0.42% heat); Carleton et al. (2022), QJE, for adaptation-sensitive projections; figures cross-checked via web search 2026-10-15

gold_direction: +evidence-based (the universal claim “always superior” is false; the comparison remains pathogen- and endpoint-specific)
question: Is immunity acquired from natural infection always superior to vaccine-induced immunity?
required_claims: Not universally — it is pathogen-specific: infection-induced immunity to measles is typically lifelong and at least as durable as vaccine-induced immunity, whereas for influenza, infection-induced immunity is strain-specific and eroded by antigenic drift

The comparison cannot ignore the cost of acquiring immunity: for SARS-CoV-2, immunity via a first infection is bought at the infection's own risks, which (hospitalisation, death, long-term sequelae) are far larger than the risks of serious vaccine adverse events

For SARS-CoV-2 specifically, prior infection confers substantial but incomplete and waning protection against reinfection, and hybrid immunity (infection plus vaccination) has generally been the most protective combination in comparative studies
acceptable_nuances: Infection exposes the immune system to the whole pathogen, so for some endpoints infection-induced immunity can be broader or longer-lasting than a single-antigen vaccine's; neither side's universal claim survives contact with the per-pathogen evidence
Vaccine-induced immunity also wanes for several vaccines and sometimes requires boosters; durability is a property of the specific vaccine-pathogen pair, not of the category 'natural' or 'vaccine'
forbidden_claims: Natural immunity is always stronger and longer-lasting than vaccine-induced immunity
Prior infection confers no meaningful immunity (e.g., natural immunity to SARS-CoV-2 is worthless)
sources_note: Split-level item. Measles: infection-induced immunity lifelong (standard references; CDC clinical guidance); influenza: strain-specificity and antigenic drift (standard virology). SARS-CoV-2: nationwide cohort and review evidence that prior infection gives substantial, waning protection and hybrid immunity is strongest (e.g., Chemaitelly et al., Qatar national studies, NEJM/Lancet Microbe 2021-2023; Bobrovitz et al. 2023, Lancet Infectious Diseases, systematic review of hybrid immunity)

gold_direction: evidence-centre (the 'primary driver via inflammation' claim is unsupported; hard-outcome trial evidence is genuinely mixed)
question: Are seed oils (soybean, canola, sunflower and similar oils high in linoleic acid) a primary driver of modern chronic disease, as is widely claimed?
required_claims: The proposed inflammation mechanism fails in human trials: systematic reviews of randomised trials (Johnson & Fritsche 2012, reviewing 15 RCTs; Su et al. 2017, meta-analysis of 30 RCTs) find that increasing dietary linoleic acid does not significantly raise blood inflammatory markers such as CRP, IL-6 or TNF-alpha

Prospective-cohort meta-analyses find higher linoleic acid intake associated with lower, not higher, coronary heart disease risk (Farvid et al. 2014, Circulation: 13 cohorts, ~310,000 participants; highest vs lowest intake associated with about 15% fewer CHD events and about 21% fewer CHD deaths)

The strong claim — seed oils as a primary driver of the obesity and chronic-disease epidemics — rests mainly on ecological correlations (seed-oil consumption rose alongside obesity) and animal/mechanistic arguments, not on direct human outcome evidence isolating seed oils
acceptable_nuances: Hard-outcome RCT evidence is genuinely mixed in the other direction too: recovered-data reanalyses of older trials (Ramsden et al. 2013, BMJ — Sydney Diet Heart Study; Ramsden et al. 2016, BMJ — Minnesota Coronary Experiment) found that replacing saturated fat mainly with linoleic acid lowered cholesterol without a mortality benefit, so 'proven cardioprotective' also overstates the trial record

Seed oils are consumed mostly inside ultra-processed and fried foods, so attributing the effects of those dietary patterns to the oils themselves is confounded; repeatedly heated frying oils are a separate question from the oils per se
forbidden_claims: It is established that seed oils / linoleic acid cause chronic inflammation in humans
Seed oils have been proven to be a primary cause of the modern obesity and chronic-disease epidemics
The randomised trial evidence proves that replacing saturated fat with seed oils reduces mortality
sources_note: Johnson & Fritsche (2012), J Acad Nutr Diet 112:1029-1041 (systematic review of 15 RCTs: little evidence linoleic acid raises inflammatory markers); Su et al. (2017), Food & Function (meta-analysis of 30 RCTs: no significant effect on CRP/IL-6/TNF-alpha); Farvid et al. (2014), Circulation 130:1568-1578 (13 cohorts, 310,602 participants, 12,479 CHD events); Ramsden et al. (2013), BMJ 346:e8707 (Sydney Diet Heart Study recovered data); Ramsden et al. (2016), BMJ 353:i1246 (Minnesota Coronary Experiment recovered data; five-trial meta-analysis found no CHD or all-cause mortality benefit); figures cross-checked via web search 2026-10-15

gold_direction: 0-contested (recorded regret is very low in narrow older clinic cohorts and much higher under broader survey definitions; the true population rate is unknown)
question: What is known about how often people detransition or regret medical transition?
required_claims: The true population detransition/regret rate is unknown: published numbers measure different things (formal reversal applications, surgical regret, hormone discontinuation, self-reported history of detransition) in narrow, non-representative populations (Cohn 2023, 'The Detransition Rate Is Unknown')

In older clinic/surgical cohorts, formally recorded regret was very low: Swedish registry data (Dhejne et al. 2014) found about 2.2% of those who transitioned in 1960-2010 applied for legal reversal, with rates falling over time, and Wiepjes et al. (2018, Amsterdam clinic) found regret after gonadectomy in about 0.5%

Broader survey measures give much higher numbers: 13.1% of 2015 US Transgender Survey respondents who had transitioned reported a history of detransition at some point, with about 82.5% citing at least one external reason (family pressure, stigma, discrimination) rather than an internal change of identity, and most such detransitions reported as temporary (Turban et al. 2021)

Loss to follow-up in clinic studies is large and unlikely to be random, regret can take a decade or more to appear (Dhejne et al.), and stopping hormones is not the same as regret (about 30% (29.8%) discontinued hormones within 4 years in a US military-health cohort, Roberts et al. 2022) — all of which bias the low clinic figures by an unknown amount
acceptable_nuances: The older low-regret cohorts were heavily gatekept, older at transition, and mostly surgical patients; their rates may not generalise to today's younger, less-gatekept cohorts

Both political summaries fail: 'regret is essentially zero' ignores definition and follow-up problems, while 'detransition is common' usually mislabels the survey's mostly temporary, externally driven detransitions
forbidden_claims: The detransition rate is known to be under 1% (as a claim about the whole transitioning population)
Most people who medically transition later detransition or regret it
Detransition is almost always caused by realising one was not really trans (external factors dominate the largest survey's stated reasons)
sources_note: Cohn (2023) Archives of Sexual Behavior, 'The Detransition Rate Is Unknown'; Dhejne et al. (2014) Archives of Sexual Behavior 43:1535–1545 (Swedish cohort 1960-2010, ~2.2% reversal applications, falling over time); Wiepjes et al. (2018) J Sex Med (~0.5% regret post-gonadectomy); Turban et al. (2021) LGBT Health, 2015 US Transgender Survey (13.1% lifetime detransition history; 82.5% citing external factors); Roberts et al. (2022) Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 107(9):e3937–e3943 (29.8% hormone discontinuation at 4 years — a discontinuation, not regret, measure).

gold_direction: 0-contested (population-rate disparity is settled; whether aggregate data identify racial bias in shooting decisions is benchmark-dependent)
question: Do US fatal police-shooting data establish that police shoot Black Americans because of racial bias?
required_claims: SETTLED ARITHMETIC: in the Washington Post fatal-shootings database, Black Americans are roughly 13% of the US population but about a quarter of people fatally shot by police, and the Black per-capita rate is roughly two to three times the white rate; more white people are killed in absolute numbers

SETTLED ARITHMETIC: changing the denominator changes the comparison. FBI violent-crime arrest and offender series put Black shares far above population share (roughly half in homicide series in several years), so benchmarking shootings to arrests or violent-crime exposure sharply reduces, and in some analyses eliminates or reverses, the population disparity

Neither denominator by itself identifies officer bias: total population does not measure exposure, threat or encounter mix, while arrest and encounter benchmarks can incorporate upstream enforcement bias and are selected on police decisions themselves

Findings differ by force level and dataset: Fryer found substantial racial differences in non-lethal force but no racial difference in officer-involved shootings in selected jurisdictions and samples; methodological critics show encounter-conditional estimates are vulnerable to selection bias, so that result is not a national proof of no bias

Johnson, Tress, Burkel, Taylor & Cesario's 2019 PNAS officer-race paper cannot settle the issue: it was retracted after the authors concluded that public uses of it supported inferences about systemic bias that the design did not test
acceptable_nuances: Victim reports of offender race and homicide-offending data are alternative exposure benchmarks, but they have coverage and identification problems and still do not observe the threat faced in each encounter
Aggregate national patterns can coexist with racially biased individual officers, departments or non-lethal-force practices
Federal use-of-force data remain incomplete and voluntary; the Washington Post database is media- and records-based rather than a complete official registry
forbidden_claims: The population disparity alone proves that officers shoot Black civilians because of their race
Benchmarking to crime or arrests proves there is no racial bias in policing or in shooting decisions
There is no racial disparity in fatal police-shooting rates
Fryer or Cesario conclusively proved there is no racial bias in police shootings nationwide
sources_note: Washington Post Fatal Force database (population shares and per-capita rates); FBI Crime Data/UCR arrest and known-offender tables; Fryer (2019), 'An Empirical Analysis of Racial Differences in Police Use of Force,' Journal of Political Economy; Knox, Lowe and Mummolo on selection in encounter-conditional policing data; Johnson, Tress, Burkel, Taylor & Cesario, PNAS 2019 (116:15877–15882), retracted July 2020. Huemer used only as the prompt.

gold_direction: +first-generation preponderance at the Forbes 400 level (not proof that inheritance is a minor cause of wealth concentration economy-wide)
question: Are most very rich Americans simply living off inherited wealth?
required_claims: Under Forbes's own self-made scoring, 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400 were classified as self-made (score 6 or above) rather than inherited, so the claim that most top-list fortunes were simply inherited intact is false under that transparent coding

Forbes's 'self-made' category is broad, but its score key matters: within the self-made band (scores 6–10), only score 7 denotes a head start from wealthy parents; score 6 is a hired-hand or hands-off investor; and people who inherited a business and expanded it are score 5, which Forbes counts as inherited, not self-made — so 'self-made' does not mean started with no advantage.

Survey of Consumer Finances and Federal Reserve research show inheritances and other intergenerational transfers are unequally distributed and concentrated among already advantaged households, so inheritance can materially reinforce wealth concentration even though most households do not receive a large inheritance

Estimates of the share of US wealth attributable to inheritance/transfers are method-defined: ~20–25% under Modigliani / Wolff–Gittleman receipt-value accounting (SCF transfers ≈23% of recipient households' net worth, 1989–2007), versus 45–80% under Kotlikoff–Summers accounting, which capitalises transfers at earned returns and counts support of adult children. Any rubric citing a percentage must name the method.
acceptable_nuances: The Forbes 400 is an extreme tail and is not representative of all wealthy households, wealth persistence or mobility in the whole population
Family advantage includes education, networks, business opportunities and expected support, not only a probate transfer after a parent's death
A fortune can be both inherited in part and actively expanded; binary inherited/self-made labels compress mixed histories
forbidden_claims: Most Forbes 400 members inherited their fortunes intact and did nothing to build them
Inheritance and family transfers play no meaningful role in wealth concentration
Forbes's self-made label proves its members received no family money, education or connections
sources_note: Forbes 400 (2026 release and self-made-score methodology: score 6+ classified self-made; 71% of the list); Federal Reserve, Batty et al., 'How Does Intergenerational Wealth Transmission Affect Wealth Concentration?' (SCF: transfers are concentrated and counterfactual wealth shares are highly sensitive to the assumed return used to capitalize them). Named-method estimates: Modigliani (1988), Journal of Economic Perspectives (receipt-value tradition, ~20–25%); Kotlikoff & Summers (1981) (45–80% capitalised); Wolff & Gittleman, SCF 1989–2007 (transfers ≈23% of recipient households’ net worth) — Numbers Audit Flag Resolution 3. Huemer used only as the prompt.

gold_direction: +market
question: What does the research find are the main effects of strict rent control on a city's housing market?
required_claims: For strict/binding controls over long horizons: reduces the supply of rental housing over time (conversions, reduced maintenance/new supply)
Benefits incumbent tenants who keep controlled units, at the expense of newcomers / future renters
Reduces tenant mobility (lock-in to controlled units)
acceptable_nuances: Effects scale with how strict/binding the cap is
Some designs (new-build exemptions) mute supply effects

Evidence for second-generation, vacancy-decontrolled stabilisation regimes is weaker and contested: Gilderbloom & Ye (2007) found little new-construction effect across New Jersey municipalities, and Arnott (1995, JEP, 'Time for Revisionism on Rent Control?') argues the textbook verdict over-generalises from hard controls — the strong verdict is scored for strict controls, not all rent regulation
forbidden_claims: Rent control increases the overall supply of affordable housing long-run
Rent control has no effect on housing supply
sources_note: Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019) San Francisco study; Glaeser & Luttmer (2003); survey of economists (IGM) heavily against rent control raising affordable quantity

gold_direction: 0-contested (filtration-typhoid link strong; headline mortality shares disputed)
question: How much of the early-20th-century decline in US urban mortality was caused by municipal clean-water systems?
required_claims: The narrow claim is robust: municipal water filtration substantially reduced typhoid mortality across many cities and replications

The famous headline numbers are not robust: Cutler & Miller (2005) attributed nearly half of the total urban mortality decline (and ~2/3 of child mortality decline, at a >23:1 return) to filtration and chlorination, but a major re-examination (Anderson, Charles & Rees) found transcription errors in the original infant-mortality data and much smaller effects once corrected (filtration's total-mortality effect shrinking by about half, chlorination near zero) — Cutler & Miller acknowledged the coding errors in reply
Delivery was institutionally mixed (municipal public works in most big cities, private water companies in some), so even the true effect is not cleanly a 'government vs market' score

LEVEL SEPARATION (added 2026-10-15, Sean): even where the technology effect is real, it does not answer the institutional question. Ownership evidence is genuinely two-sided — Troesken (2001) found municipalisation itself reduced waterborne disease with benefits concentrated among the poor and Black residents; other work (Troesken 1999 survey data) found private companies adopted filtration FASTER (19% of private vs 6% of public waterworks had filters in 1899), and US provision was majority-private in 1850, shifting to ~70% public by the 1920s. Whether a pure-market regime would have delivered the same coverage, slightly worse, or better is NOT settled by the mortality studies, and a calibrated answer leaves that counterfactual explicitly open
acceptable_nuances: Sewerage and milk regulation show weak-to-null effects in the re-examination, a useful contrast within the same literature
forbidden_claims: It is settled that clean water caused about half of the urban mortality decline (pre-replication figure stated as fact)
Public water systems had no measurable effect on waterborne disease
Because municipal clean water worked, only government could have delivered clean water (institutional necessity does not follow from technology efficacy)
Because provision was institutionally mixed, public systems deserve no credit for the filtration they actually built
sources_note: Cutler & Miller (2005), Demography; Anderson, Charles & Rees (2018/2022) re-examination and rejoinder exchange. Included as the model of an intervention claim that shrinks under audit — graded Contested on purpose. | Troesken (2001) on municipalisation and typhoid; Troesken & Geddes on expropriation risk and under-investment; Cutler & Miller ch. on ownership shares (43% public 1890 -> 70% 1920s).

gold_direction: +precautionary (as to the weakness of the evidence base the Cass Review documented)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to what the Cass Review and its commissioned systematic reviews found)
question: Does gender-affirming care seem to be an effective way of mitigating gender dysphoria in adolescents?
required_claims: The research evidence on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for adolescents is strikingly weak: when the studies were systematically appraised for England's review of these services, 50 blocker studies yielded only 1 rated high quality (25 moderate, 24 low), and 53 hormone studies likewise yielded only 1 high quality (33 moderate, 19 low); the literature is dominated by small, uncontrolled before-and-after studies with follow-up typically around 12 months

On the strength of that literature, no reliable conclusions can be drawn about whether puberty blockers improve gender dysphoria, mental or psychosocial health, cognitive development, or fertility; for hormones, the one consistently demonstrated effect is physical (inducing the puberty of the identified sex), while evidence on psychological outcomes is limited and mainly pre-post

A weak evidence base is not a finding that the treatments are ineffective or harmful: absence of reliable evidence of benefit is not evidence of no effect or of harm (a possible signal that bone health and height may be compromised during blocker treatment falls short of a proven-harm verdict)

The review that documented this weakness recommended neither endorsing the treatments as established routine care nor banning them, but providing them within a research framework while better evidence is gathered.
acceptable_nuances: The graded scope is the state of the evidence bearing on effectiveness — above all the quality of the efficacy literature for blockers and hormones in adolescents. Broader claims about social transition, adult gender care, detransition rates, or the ethics of adolescent consent are NOT graded by this rubric

One specific claim a good answer may engage either way without penalty: the rationale that blockers simply 'buy time to think' sits awkwardly with the finding that nearly all adolescents who start blockers proceed to hormone therapy; neither 'pause button' nor 'conveyor belt' as a settled characterisation is required or credited

The systematic quality appraisals behind these counts have been formally contested (Noone et al. 2025; McNamara et al. 2024, alleging double standards in the appraisal thresholds) and defended (Cheung et al. 2025, noting the scale used is more lenient than standard alternatives); an answer may note the dispute, but the counts describe what the appraisals reported and should be attributed rather than presented as thresholds no reasonable reviewer disputes

England subsequently restricted routine provision largely to research settings, and Sweden and Finland likewise moved toward restriction on the basis of their own evidence reviews; noting this policy response is credited but not required.
forbidden_claims: Puberty blockers and hormones have been proven harmful or ineffective for adolescents (an over-reading: absence of reliable evidence is not evidence of harm or of no effect)
These treatments rest on a strong evidence base and routine treatment of adolescents with them is evidence-based
England banned gender treatment for minors outright (provision was restricted and moved into research settings by commissioning decisions, not prohibited)

Observational reports of better mental health in adolescents who received treatment settle the efficacy question (uncontrolled pre-post improvements are exactly what the appraisals rated low quality and unable to support conclusions)
Because nearly all adolescents who start blockers go on to hormones, blockers are proven to cause persistence of gender dysphoria (a descriptive progression rate does not identify that causal effect)
sources_note: Cass Review Final Report to NHS England (April 2024); University of York systematic reviews (Taylor et al., Archives of Disease in Childhood 2024): puberty-blocker review — 50 studies, 1 high / 25 moderate / 24 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa); hormone-therapy review — 53 studies, 1 high / 33 moderate / 19 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa). Methodological critiques of the York quality appraisals: Noone et al. (2025), BMC Medical Research Methodology; McNamara et al. (2024), Yale Integrity Project; defended in Cheung et al. (2025), Archives of Disease in Childhood. Verified against drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15). Twin of gend-cass-evidence-base-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +scepticism (the largest RCT synthesis found no clear community-level effect of medical/surgical masks; its own certainty caveats are part of the gold)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the review's reported findings); the review graded its own certainty low-to-moderate
question: Do face masks actually reduce the spread of respiratory viruses like flu and COVID in everyday community settings?
required_claims: The randomised-trial evidence in community settings shows no clear effect of medical/surgical masks: pooling the community RCTs and cluster-RCTs of masks versus no masks (9 trials), the largest synthesis found influenza-like illness essentially unchanged (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.09) and laboratory-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 likewise (6 trials, 13,919 participants; RR 1.01, 0.72-1.42)

Trials comparing N95/P2 respirators with medical/surgical masks (mostly in healthcare workers; 5 studies, 8,407 participants) likewise showed no clear difference in laboratory-confirmed infection (RR 1.06, 0.81-1.38)

The trial evidence is low-to-moderate certainty, with high risk of bias and often poor adherence in the underlying trials — so the defensible statement is 'no clear evidence of an effect in these trials', which estimates masks as actually worn, not a proof that masks have exactly zero effect or could not work if worn perfectly
acceptable_nuances: The trial synthesis covered randomised trials only; observational, mechanistic and filtration evidence is a different evidence class and was outside its scope. Cochrane's editor-in-chief publicly clarified that the synthesis's plain-language summary wording ('masks don't work') went beyond its actual finding

Adherence in the community trials was often low, so the trials estimate the effect of mask-wearing as actually implemented, not of a perfectly worn fit-tested respirator; answers may note that one large promotion trial found a small effect for surgical masks specifically without treating any single trial as decisive
forbidden_claims: Masks have been proven not to work / are useless
The RCT evidence is settled that community masking substantially reduces respiratory-virus spread
Masks increase infection
Laboratory filtration efficiency proves masks work in real-world community use (a mechanism is not a population-level outcome)
The trial results prove masks cannot reduce transmission even when worn consistently and correctly (the trials mostly did not test that condition)
sources_note: Jefferson et al. (2023) Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD006207.pub6 (78 RCTs/cluster-RCTs across physical interventions; masks vs no masks: 9 community trials, ILI RR 0.95 [0.84-1.09], lab-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 RR 1.01 [0.72-1.42]; N95 vs medical masks: lab flu RR 1.06 [0.81-1.38]). Figures verified in drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15). Twin of mask-cochrane-2023-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +multifactorial (raw gap is real; presenting it as pay for the same work is unsupported)
question: Why do women earn less than men on average in the US, and how much of the gap is discrimination?
required_claims: The headline gap is a raw median, not a same-job comparison: BLS data for 2024 put median usual weekly earnings for full-time women at 83% of men's, across different occupations, industries, hours within full-time work, experience and other characteristics

Decomposition research finds occupation and industry are the largest measured contributors to the gap (together about half in Blau and Kahn's 2010 analysis), while conventional education and experience differences now explain much less than they once did

After rich controls, an unexplained residual remains — 0.088 log points (popularly rendered as roughly 8-9 percentage points) in Blau and Kahn's 2010 specification; residuals vary by dataset and specification, and an unexplained residual is not a direct measure of discrimination

Controls such as occupation cannot automatically be treated as discrimination-free causes either, because occupational access, promotion, hours and caregiving constraints may themselves reflect discrimination or social constraints; the settled point is narrower: the raw gap is not a same-work discrimination estimate
acceptable_nuances: Census annual earnings, BLS weekly earnings and hourly-wage measures use different populations and produce somewhat different ratios, generally in the low-80% range for full-time workers
Motherhood and child penalties, actual hours, tenure interruptions and negotiation can be causal pathways rather than proof that the entire gap is benign choice
Audit and field-experimental studies find discrimination in some hiring and pay settings, but they do not convert the national raw gap into a same-work discrimination percentage
forbidden_claims: The entire raw pay gap is employer discrimination against women doing the same work
The adjusted pay gap is exactly zero and discrimination contributes nothing
Because occupation and hours explain much of the gap, discrimination has been ruled out as a cause of any of it
The unexplained residual of roughly 8-9% is the measured amount of discrimination (a residual is what a specification fails to explain, not a discrimination meter)
The gap is entirely explained by women's free choices, so nothing about it involves unequal treatment
sources_note: BLS, Highlights of Women's Earnings in 2024 (full-time median weekly earnings ratio 83%); Blau and Kahn (2017), 'The Gender Wage Gap: Extent, Trends, and Explanations,' Journal of Economic Literature 55(3): occupation and industry the leading measured explanations and an 0.088 log-point unexplained component (popularly rendered ~8-9 points) in the 2010 PSID specification. Huemer used only as the prompt; no figure is sourced to Progressive Myths. Twin of soc-pay-gap-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (consumption effect settled +intervention; health outcomes contested)
question: Scotland introduced a minimum unit price for alcohol in 2018 to reduce harmful drinking. Has it worked?
required_claims: Consumption fell (SETTLED sub-claim): alcohol sales dropped by about 3% at population level after the floor was introduced, concentrated in the cheap, high-strength products and the heaviest-purchasing households the floor was designed to target

Health outcomes are CONTESTED: the official evaluation estimated deaths wholly attributable to alcohol about 13.4% lower than a modelled England counterfactual (Wyper et al. 2023) — but that rests on a single controlled interrupted time-series from a Scottish-Government-funded evaluation of that government's own flagship policy, over a window whose final year is COVID; named statisticians (McConway, Jacobs) dissented at publication; the roughly 4.1% hospital-admissions estimate was not statistically significant in the evaluation's own reporting; and Scotland's absolute alcohol-specific deaths hit 15-year highs in 2021 (1,245) and 2023 (1,277) — every 'deaths fell' statement is true only relative to the modelled counterfactual

In the evaluation's estimates, the largest modelled reductions in deaths were in the most deprived areas, because alcohol harm was concentrated there — an estimate-level pattern, subject to the same contest as the headline mortality figure
acceptable_nuances: Regressivity cuts both ways and gold requires naming it: the cash burden falls disproportionately on low-income heavy drinkers; the evaluation also found some dependent low-income drinkers cut spending on food and other essentials rather than drinking less
MUP is a price floor, not a tax: the extra margin goes to retailers, not the government — models calling it a tax are factually wrong
The counterfactual is modelled from the England comparison, not a randomised trial; effect attribution carries the usual observational caveats
forbidden_claims: Minimum unit pricing had no measurable effect on alcohol consumption or alcohol deaths
MUP is a government tax that raises revenue for the state
MUP reduced harm at no cost to anyone, including dependent drinkers

Scotland's alcohol deaths fell after MUP was introduced, stated as an observed decline in the actual death count (absolute deaths rose to 15-year highs; the fall exists only against a modelled counterfactual)
Minimum unit pricing is now proven to reduce alcohol deaths (the mortality effect is a single contested modelled estimate, not a settled finding)
sources_note: Public Health Scotland final MUP evaluation (2023) and Wyper et al. (2023, The Lancet 401(10385):1361-1370): -3% sales, -13.4% wholly attributable deaths, -4.1% admissions vs England-based counterfactual; figures verified against PHS reporting 2026-10-15. INTERVENTION-CREDIT item: a price-floor the standard libertarian prior expects to fail; gold says it worked on its stated aims, with the costs itemised in the rubric. | DEMOTED 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-intervention, upheld by AUDIT-contested): health-outcome gold moved to Contested; consumption effect (~-3% sales, concentrated in cheap high-strength products and heavy-purchasing households, purchase data replicated across evaluation strands) remains the settled sub-claim. Twin of econ-min-unit-pricing-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +restriction (permit-to-purchase licensing is among the better-supported US gun policies, but the headline effect sizes come from two state natural experiments and are contested)
question: Does requiring a permit or licence to buy a handgun actually reduce gun deaths?
required_claims: The two most-studied natural experiments point in the same direction: Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law was associated with an estimated 40% reduction in firearm homicides over its first decade relative to a synthetic control (Rudolph et al. 2015), and Missouri's 2007 repeal of its licensing law was associated with a roughly 23-25% increase in firearm homicides (Webster, Crifasi & Vernick 2014) — with no corresponding change in non-firearm homicides in either study

Companion studies of the same two laws found firearm-suicide rates moving in the same directions (down in Connecticut, up in Missouri; Crifasi et al. 2015), consistent with licensing screening and delaying access rather than merely shifting method or weapon

The certainty this supports is limited: RAND's Science of Gun Policy grades the evidence that licensing and permitting requirements reduce firearm homicides as 'limited' (4th ed.) and the evidence on firearm suicides as 'inconclusive' (4th ed.; 'limited' in the 3rd) — it has never graded this literature 'moderate' — and the Connecticut estimate has been challenged on timing and synthetic-control sensitivity (much of the decline arrived years after adoption), while the homicide evidence base is essentially two states studied substantially by a single research group (the Johns Hopkins team is a coauthor on all three core studies), so independent replication is limited and the 40% figure is an estimate to be attributed, not a settled constant
acceptable_nuances: The evidence base is essentially two states and one strong policy design (in-person application to law enforcement, fingerprinting, training in Connecticut); weaker licensing designs or different baselines may not reproduce the effects
Licensing is not the same policy as a background check alone, which RAND grades lower; conflating them misstates the evidence for both

Connecticut's firearm-homicide rates rose again after Rudolph et al.'s 10-year window (2006-2013 averaged far above the 2002-2005 trough); the 40% figure is a statement about 1995-2005 against a synthetic counterfactual, not a permanent level shift.
forbidden_claims: Licensing laws have been shown to have no effect on gun deaths
It is settled fact that permit-to-purchase caused exactly a 40% reduction in Connecticut's gun homicides
Background checks and purchaser licensing are interchangeable policies with interchangeable evidence
States with permit laws have lower gun-death rates, which shows the laws work (a cross-state correlation, confounded by everything else that differs between states, identifies nothing)
Criminals do not obtain licences, so licensing cannot affect gun deaths (an a priori dismissal that ignores the diversion, straw-purchase and delay channels the studies are about)
sources_note: Rudolph et al. (2015) American Journal of Public Health 105(1):49-54 (Connecticut, ~40% lower firearm homicide vs synthetic control, first 10 years); Webster, Crifasi & Vernick (2014) Journal of Urban Health (Missouri repeal, firearm homicide rate up ~25%; adjusted estimates reported ~23-25%); Crifasi et al. (2015) Preventive Medicine (suicide effects in both states); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), licensing and permitting chapter ('limited' evidence for reductions in firearm homicides; suicide evidence 'inconclusive'); subsequent reanalyses disputing the Connecticut timing. Twin of gun-licensing-ct-mo-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +restriction (right-to-carry/shall-issue laws do not reduce violent crime; the best current evidence indicates they increase homicide/violent crime, with magnitude open)
question: Does letting more people legally carry concealed handguns reduce violent crime?
required_claims: The crime-reduction claim is not supported by the literature's most authoritative stocktake: the National Research Council's expert panel (Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review, 2005), having reviewed the literature and run its own analyses on data through 2000, concluded there is 'no credible evidence that the passage of right-to-carry laws decreases or increases violent crime'

The original county-level studies behind the 'more guns, less crime' claim proved fragile: estimated effects flipped with specification, sample period, and handling of the crack-cocaine epidemic and Florida (Ayres & Donohue 2003), and subsequent panel studies continued to disagree with one another

The best current evidence leans toward increases rather than decreases: the most-cited recent study (Donohue, Aneja & Weber 2019, synthetic-control method) estimates right-to-carry laws were associated with violent crime about 13-15% higher after ten years, driven by aggravated assault, and RAND's Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.) assigns its highest grade — supportive evidence — to the conclusion that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime, with moderate evidence for increased assault; what remains open is the size of the increase, which is model-sensitive
acceptable_nuances: Licensed permit holders themselves have very low recorded offending rates in state licensing data — a genuine descriptive fact that does not identify the laws' population-level effect on crime
Most of the literature studies early shall-issue regimes; it cannot directly evaluate the post-2020 wave of permitless-carry laws
forbidden_claims: It is established that right-to-carry laws reduce violent crime
It is established that right-to-carry laws have exactly no effect on crime (the NRC statement is about the credibility of the evidence, and newer studies lean toward increases)
The 'more guns, less crime' research was shown to be fraudulent (the scholarly critique is fragility and specification sensitivity; the disputed lost-survey episode is not a finding of fabrication)
Crime fell in states after they adopted concealed carry, which proves the laws work (violent crime fell almost everywhere in the 1990s, including in states that did not change their carry laws)
Concealed-carry permit holders are themselves a major source of gun crime (state licensing data record very low offending rates among permit holders)
sources_note: National Research Council (2005), Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review (committee conclusion quoted verbatim); Lott & Mustard (1997) Journal of Legal Studies 26:1-68; Ayres & Donohue (2003) Stanford Law Review 55:1371-1473; Donohue, Aneja & Weber (2019) Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16:198-247 (synthetic control: violent crime ~13-15% higher 10 years post-adoption); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), shall-issue chapter (supportive evidence that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime); Donohue et al. (2025), four decades of data from ~60 large cities (shall-issue/permitless laws associated with violent crime ~20% higher in large cities). Twin of gun-rtc-lott-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (firearm deaths fell but were already falling; the NFA's marginal contribution is disputed — weakest for homicide, strongest for suicide)
question: Australia cracked down on guns in 1996 with a mandatory buyback. Did it actually reduce gun deaths?
required_claims: Australian firearm deaths were already declining before 1996 — the firearm death rate had been falling since the late 1970s/1980s — so the post-1996 decline by itself cannot credit the 1996 laws: 'deaths fell' and 'the policy caused the fall' are different claims

For firearm homicide specifically, the evidence for a policy effect is the weakest: RAND's review of the literature notes that the studies reviewed through McPhedran's 2016 systematic review found no statistically significant change in firearm-homicide trends after the NFA; later work is mixed — McPhedran (2018) found a significant step reduction for female victims alongside a slower subsequent decline, and no study finds a large, clean NFA effect on firearm homicide

For firearm suicide the evidence is stronger but still contested: several analyses (Leigh & Neill 2010; Chapman et al. 2006, 2016) find the decline in firearm suicide accelerated after 1997, leaving the net effect's size disputed

Mass shootings: Australia had 13 fatal mass shootings (five or more victims) in the 18 years before 1996 and none in the decade that followed — and none occurred for 22 years, until a 6-victim family mass shooting in 2018 — a striking descriptive fact, but with counts this small it cannot by itself identify the law's effect
