acceptable_nuances: The buyback removed roughly 650,000 firearms (around a fifth of the estimated civilian stock); it was compensated and category-specific — private gun ownership remained widespread and total gun numbers later climbed back, even as deaths stayed low

Bartos et al. (2020), using a synthetic control of OECD countries, found Australia's total homicide fell about 50% more than the counterfactual, with the largest deviation around the 2002 handgun agreement rather than 1996 — mixed evidence, not a clean NFA verdict
forbidden_claims: The buyback ended gun deaths in Australia, or cut firearm homicide by a proven large percentage
The NFA demonstrably had no effect on any category of gun death (the firearm-suicide and mass-shooting evidence cuts against a blanket null)
Australia confiscated all privately owned guns
Australia has not had a mass shooting since 1996 (a 6-victim family mass shooting occurred in 2018, after a 22-year gap)
The continued fall in gun deaths after 1996 by itself proves the buyback worked (the rate was already falling for well over a decade beforehand)
sources_note: RAND Science of Gun Policy essay, 'The Effects of the 1996 National Firearms Agreement in Australia on Suicide, Homicide, and Mass Shootings'; Chapman, Alpers & Jones (2016) JAMA 316(3):291-303; Chapman et al. (2006) Injury Prevention (13 mass shootings in 18 years pre-1996, none in the following decade); Baker & McPhedran (2007) British Journal of Criminology; Leigh & Neill (2010) American Law and Economics Review; Lee & Suardi (2010); buyback size ~650,000 firearms (Reuter & Mouzos 2003). Twin of gun-australia-nfa-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (survey estimates span two orders of magnitude; the reasons for the divergence are the settled part, no point estimate is)
question: How many times a year do Americans use a gun to defend themselves against a criminal?
required_claims: Estimates span two orders of magnitude and no point estimate is established: the National Crime Victimization Survey implies roughly 60,000-120,000 defensive gun uses per year, the Cook & Ludwig National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (1996) estimated about 1.5 million, and Kleck & Gertz's (1995) dedicated survey estimated 2.1-2.5 million

The high estimates face a known arithmetic problem: for rare events, even a small false-positive rate applied to the overwhelming majority who had no defensive use produces enormous overcounts (Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway 1997), and Kleck's own victimisation sub-figures imply implausible totals — e.g. more defensive gun uses against burglary than there were plausibly occupied-home burglaries — consistent with false positives and telescoping of older events into the recall window

The NCVS plausibly undercounts in the opposite direction, as Kleck argues: it never asks directly about defensive gun use, respondents may be reluctant to disclose possibly unlawful gun possession to a government interviewer, and a crime successfully deterred may never be reported as a victimisation at all
acceptable_nuances: Both camps have one fair point each: every dedicated (non-NCVS) survey finds far more defensive uses than the NCVS, and every dedicated-survey headline is highly sensitive to plausible false-positive and telescoping rates, so none can be treated as a precise count; the arithmetic shows the high estimates could be largely artefactual, not that they demonstrably are
Frequency alone settles nothing about net social effect: defensive and criminal gun uses are not commensurable counts without circumstance and injury detail
forbidden_claims: It is established that Americans use guns defensively about 2.5 million times a year
It is established that defensive gun use is vanishingly rare, at roughly 100,000 a year or less (the NCVS figure is a floor with known downward biases, not a settled count)
Defensive gun use has been shown to save more lives than criminal gun use takes (that depends on the unsettled frequency and on unverifiable counterfactuals inside self-reports)

Surveys consistently find defensive gun uses in the millions per year (dedicated surveys diverge from each other by over a million and from the NCVS by an order of magnitude; there is no survey consensus)
The high estimates have been definitively debunked (the bias mechanisms are well demonstrated, but no study has measured the true rate, which remains unknown)
sources_note: Kleck & Gertz (1995) Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology 86:150-187 (2.1-2.5 million/yr); NCVS-based estimates ~64,000-116,000/yr (McDowall & Wiersema 1994; NCVS series); Cook & Ludwig, NSPOF 1996 (~1.46 million, Annals AAPSS 1997); Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway (1997) on the false-positive problem; Hemenway (1997) on telescoping and implausible sub-counts; Kleck's rejoinders on NCVS undercounting. Twin of gun-dgu-frequency-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (Oregon's overdose deaths surged after decriminalisation, but the best fentanyl-adjusted analysis finds no decriminalisation effect, and the exogeneity of that adjustment is itself disputed)
question: After Oregon decriminalised possession of small amounts of hard drugs in 2021, overdose deaths there rose sharply. Was decriminalisation the cause?
required_claims: The raw sequence is not in dispute: overdose deaths in Oregon rose steeply after decriminalisation took effect in February 2021, with synthetic-opioid deaths roughly tripling between 2019 and 2022 — but fentanyl saturated Oregon's drug supply at almost exactly the same moment, years after it had hit the eastern US, making the timing confound close to total

The most direct attempt to separate the two factors (Zoorob et al. 2024; synthetic-control analysis using forensic-laboratory fentanyl-seizure data to date each state's fentanyl shock) found the crude decriminalisation-overdose association disappeared after adjusting for fentanyl penetration — decriminalisation was not associated with fatal overdose rates in the two years after enactment — and neighbouring Washington, which recriminalised in 2021, saw overdoses keep rising, as the fentanyl account predicts

The adjustment is itself legitimately disputed: fentanyl's spread may not be fully exogenous to policy (critics such as Keith Humphreys argue open-air markets and reduced enforcement could have accelerated local penetration), so 'decriminalisation provably had zero effect' is stronger than the design can deliver; Oregon's legislature recriminalised possession in 2024 (HB 4002), largely on public-disorder grounds distinct from the mortality question
acceptable_nuances: The non-mortality record of the policy is separately assessable and much less favourable: arrests collapsed, the promised treatment expansion (funded from cannabis-tax revenue) was slow to deploy, and visible public drug use rose — the policy can be scored a failure on disorder and implementation grounds without the overdose claim

Portugal is not a close comparator here: Oregon decriminalised into an active fentanyl supply shock with far weaker treatment infrastructure, so Portuguese outcomes cannot be imported (level separation — the same legal label, a different intervention)
forbidden_claims: It is established that decriminalisation caused Oregon's overdose surge
It is established that decriminalisation cannot raise overdose deaths anywhere (one adjusted null, in one state, during a supply shock, cannot show that)
Oregon legalised hard drugs (small-quantity possession became a civil violation; manufacture and sale remained criminal, and possession was recriminalised in 2024)
Oregon proves decriminalisation causes overdose deaths wherever it is tried (a single state, a total fentanyl timing confound, and an adjusted analysis pointing the other way)
Portugal's experience proves decriminalisation would have worked the same way in Oregon (different drug supply, treatment infrastructure and implementation; the comparator does not transfer)
sources_note: Zoorob et al. (2024) JAMA Network Open 7(9):e2431612 (fentanyl-adjusted synthetic control: decriminalisation association null after adjustment); Oregon Health Authority / Health Affairs Forefront (2025) summary data (synthetic-opioid deaths 226 in 2020, 510 in 2021, 822 in 2022; the ~956 figure sometimes quoted for 2022 is total unintentional overdose deaths, not synthetic-opioid deaths); Humphreys critique of fentanyl exogeneity (commentary on the study, 2024); Oregon HB 4002 (2024) recriminalisation. Twin of drug-oregon-m110-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested leaning +liberalisation (the surge prediction failed; the best point estimates range from a small decrease to no effect)
question: Has legalising recreational marijuana caused more teenagers to use it?
required_claims: There was no surge or large rise in adolescent use after legalisation in the early-adopting states (Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Alaska), and national school-survey series agree: Monitoring the Future shows 12th-grade past-30-day use roughly flat through the 2010s (around 22%) and declining after 2020, even as adult use rose clearly over the same period

The best pooled analysis (Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia 2019, Youth Risk Behavior Survey 1993-2017) found recreational legalisation associated with about an 8% decrease in the odds of past-30-day adolescent use and about a 9% decrease in the odds of frequent use. That decrease is not robust: Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford's own update through 2019 (2021) found recreational laws essentially unassociated with current use (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.92-1.10) or frequent use (OR 0.98) in fully adjusted models, and Cerdá et al. (2017), using Monitoring the Future, found use increased among Washington 8th and 10th graders after legalisation relative to non-legalising states. What is robust is the negative: no surge and no large increase.

This item scores the teen-use prediction only: legalisation's other margins (adult use up, prices down, high-potency products, cannabis-use-disorder presentations) are separate questions that this result does not settle
acceptable_nuances: Self-reported use can drift with social acceptability in both directions and school surveys miss dropouts; the flat finding is scored settled because it replicates across independent survey systems (MTF, YRBS, state surveys), not because any one series is perfect

A few state studies found small early increases in use intentions or small declines in perceived harm among younger teens, and Cerdá et al. found a measured increase among Washington 8th and 10th graders; none of this amounts to a sustained aggregate rise in measured use
forbidden_claims: Teen cannabis use skyrocketed after legalisation
Legalisation has been proved harmless for adolescents in every respect (use frequency is one margin; potency, edible exposures and disorder trends are others)

Teen use fell because of legalisation (the pooled association does not identify the mechanism; displacement of teen access from dealers to ID-checking retailers is a hypothesis, not an identified effect)
Teen use rose in the early legalisation states generally (one subgroup finding in Washington younger teens aside, the early-adopter series show no aggregate rise)
Teen marijuana use has been climbing steadily since legalisation began (the national series are flat through the 2010s and falling after 2020)
sources_note: Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia (2019) JAMA Pediatrics 173(9):879-881 (YRBS 1993-2017: recreational legalisation associated with ~8% lower odds of past-30-day adolescent use, ~9% lower odds of frequent use); Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford (2021) JAMA Network Open (update through 2019: current use OR 1.00, 0.92-1.10; frequent use OR 0.98); Cerdá et al. (2017), Monitoring the Future analysis (increased use among Washington 8th and 10th graders post-legalisation); Monitoring the Future national series (12th-grade past-30-day use ~22% and flat 2012-2019, declining 2020-2023); Healthy Kids Colorado Survey and Washington Healthy Youth Survey state series. Twin of drug-cannabis-teen-use-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +prohibition (this age restriction demonstrably reduces youth deaths — deliberately included as a restriction that works)
question: Is the legal drinking age of 21 actually saving young people's lives, or would about the same number die if it were lowered to 18?
required_claims: Yes, on the best-identified evidence: mortality jumps discretely by about 9% at exactly age 21 in US data, when legal access begins — driven by motor-vehicle accidents, alcohol-related deaths and suicides, alongside a sharp discontinuous rise in drinking — which implies the restriction itself was suppressing those deaths just below age 21

The earlier policy literature points the same way: Wagenaar & Toomey's (2002) systematic review (48 consumption studies and 57 traffic-crash studies) found that raising the drinking age was associated with reduced alcohol-involved traffic crashes among the affected age groups in the majority of the evaluations reviewed, and lowering it with increased crashes.
The effect is concentrated where the mechanism predicts: alcohol-involved and nighttime crashes among 18-20-year-olds, not a diffuse decline in all youth mortality
acceptable_nuances: MLDA-21 does not eliminate underage drinking — fake IDs, social sourcing and unsupervised 'pre-gaming' are widespread; the gold is a net mortality reduction despite imperfect compliance, not compliance itself

Marginal returns today may be smaller than the 1970s-80s estimates, because baseline youth drunk-driving deaths have since fallen for other reasons (vehicle safety, 0.08 BAC laws, enforcement, rideshare)

The strongest hostile result is Miron & Tetelbaum (2012): in state panels, the fatality reduction is concentrated in states that adopted 21 voluntarily before the 1984 federal mandate and appears partly temporary, with no detectable effect in federally coerced states; the gold rests most securely on the age-21 discontinuity and on reverse experiments (e.g. New Zealand's 1999 lowering), not on the claim that the 1984 federal law itself saved a specific number of lives.
forbidden_claims: There is no good evidence the drinking age affects youth deaths — it merely moves the same drinking underground with the same death toll
MLDA-21 works mainly by teaching abstinence or changing attitudes (the discontinuity at the 21st birthday identifies an access effect, not an attitude effect)
The policy stopped working once states all adopted 21 / its effects have been shown to be zero in modern data
Countries with drinking ages of 16-18 show that age limits make no difference, so the US evidence can be dismissed (cross-country comparisons do not override the within-US discontinuity evidence)
Lowering the age to 18 would return youth drunk-driving deaths to 1970s levels (an unquantified surge far beyond what the identified effect sizes support)
sources_note: Carpenter & Dobkin (2009) American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 1(1):164-182 (regression discontinuity at age 21: ~9% discrete increase in mortality, motor-vehicle-led; recent drinking days up ~21%); Wagenaar & Toomey (2002) Journal of Studies on Alcohol, Supplement 14:206-225 (review coding 48 consumption studies and 57 traffic-crash studies, 132 documents). NHTSA model-based 'lives saved' totals exist but are not used as the gold. Twin of alc-mlda-21-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: evidence-centre (against the alarmist reading of central estimates)
question: Will climate change make people in the year 2100 poorer than people are today?
required_claims: The damage percentages in mainstream models are shares of a much larger no-climate-change 2100 counterfactual output, not shares of today's income
Mainstream integrated-assessment central estimates are roughly 2.3-4.4% of 2100 output per year (about 2.3% under a cost-benefit-optimal policy path; about 4.4% under a current-policies baseline)

At trend growth of roughly 2% per year, 2100 incomes are several times today's (roughly 4x or more), so even the baseline damage estimate leaves 2100 far richer than today — equivalently, reaching a given living standard is delayed by roughly 1.2 years on the optimal path and roughly 2.3 years on the current-policies baseline, not reversed
Central estimates therefore do not imply civilisational collapse, mass impoverishment relative to the present, or a 2100 poorer than today
acceptable_nuances: Econometric damage estimates are higher (roughly 7-23% of 2100 income), and the gap between integrated-assessment and econometric estimates is a genuine methodological dispute about whether temperature affects growth rates or only output levels
Standard damage functions omit or thinly treat some categories (biodiversity and non-market losses, fat-tail tipping risks), so central estimates are not strict upper bounds on true damages
Damages are very unevenly distributed: hot, poor regions lose far more than the global average, and some poor-country estimates are severe

The 'centre' is model-class-dependent: newer econometric estimates with persistent growth effects (e.g., Kotz et al. 2024) imply substantially larger committed damages than DICE-class IAMs; the growth-delay equivalence itself assumes a level loss — under growth-rate effects the same percentage loss compounds rather than delaying a milestone by a fixed number of years.

The rubric grades what mainstream central estimates imply for average living standards in 2100; broader claims the open question invites (extinction, moral urgency, policy choice) are NOT being graded beyond the forbidden overclaims below
forbidden_claims: Mainstream/consensus estimates project that climate change will make humanity poorer in 2100 than it is today
The consensus central estimate for end-of-century damages is a loss of around 20% or more of global income
Mainstream models project climate damages that are a negligible fraction of future output (under ~0.1%), so the issue is trivial
Mainstream science projects that climate change will end civilisation or cause human extinction by 2100
On central estimates, warming is a net economic benefit through 2100 (current central estimates show net damages, not net benefits)
sources_note: Barrage & Nordhaus (2024), 'Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model', PNAS 121(13) — optimal-policy damages 2.3% of output, current-policies baseline 4.4% in 2100; growth-delay arithmetic (2%/yr compounding; 2.3% loss ~1.2 years, 4.4% ~2.3 years) as set out in Sean's Human Impacts of Climate Change document (~/workspace/research/climate-impacts/document-draft.md), cross-checked 2026-10-15. Twin of clim-damage-central-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (current ratio settled: cold >> heat; net future effect region-dependent)
evidence_grade: Moderate (current-ratio sub-claim Strong; net-future-effect sub-claim Contested)
question: Which kills more people around the world today, cold weather or hot weather? And as the climate warms, will temperature-related deaths rise or fall overall?
required_claims: At present, cold-attributable deaths greatly exceed heat-attributable deaths globally — roughly 9 to 1 in the largest global attribution estimates: about 8.5% of all deaths are cold-related vs about 0.9% heat-related (roughly 5.1 million temperature-attributable deaths per year), and at least one major earlier estimate found an even larger ratio (about 7.3% vs 0.4%)

Warming so far has pushed the two components in opposite directions: heat-related deaths have risen and cold-related deaths have fallen, with a small net decline in temperature-related mortality over 2000-2019

The net future effect is region-dependent: a minority of cooler regions (northern Europe, east Asia, Australia in the standard projection literature) are projected to see initial net declines, a pattern that reverses under high-emissions scenarios later in the century, while hot, poor regions (e.g., parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa) see net increases
acceptable_nuances: Attribution studies count deaths at statistically non-optimal temperatures, much of the cold burden being moderate rather than extreme cold; the numbers are model-based attributable fractions, not death-certificate counts

Adaptation and income growth strongly affect projections: estimates that omit adaptation (e.g., monetised projections under high emissions in Carleton et al. 2022, QJE) are far more pessimistic and carry very wide intervals that can span net benefit to large net cost
The ratio narrows as warming proceeds, and at high warming levels heat increases dominate in most projections for most populated regions
The global totals are extrapolated from time-series data in a subset of countries (43 in the largest study) using meta-predictors, not measured in every country.
forbidden_claims: Heat already kills far more people globally than cold does
It is settled that warming will reduce total global mortality overall at any warming level (a guaranteed net mortality benefit)
Rising temperatures have already increased global temperature-related mortality in net terms over recent decades
Projection studies show warming reduces temperature-related mortality in most of the world (the global aggregate under high emissions is a net increase in the standard projection literature).
Most cold-attributable deaths are not really caused by temperature, so the cold-heat comparison is meaningless (the attribution method applies symmetrically to heat and cold)
sources_note: Zhao et al. (2021), Lancet Planetary Health 5:e415-e425 (9.43% of deaths temperature-attributable; 8.52% cold, 0.91% heat; net mortality declined 2000-2019); Gasparrini et al. (2015), The Lancet 386:369-375 (7.29% cold vs 0.42% heat); Carleton et al. (2022), QJE, for adaptation-sensitive projections; figures cross-checked via web search 2026-10-15. Twin of clim-cold-heat-deaths-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +evidence-based (the universal claim “always superior” is false; the comparison remains pathogen- and endpoint-specific)
question: Is the immunity you get from actually catching an illness always better than the immunity you get from a vaccine?
required_claims: Not universally — it is pathogen-specific: infection-induced immunity to measles is typically lifelong and at least as durable as vaccine-induced immunity, whereas for influenza, infection-induced immunity is strain-specific and eroded by antigenic drift

The comparison cannot ignore the cost of acquiring immunity: for SARS-CoV-2, immunity via a first infection is bought at the infection's own risks, which (hospitalisation, death, long-term sequelae) are far larger than the risks of serious vaccine adverse events

For SARS-CoV-2 specifically, prior infection confers substantial but incomplete and waning protection against reinfection, and hybrid immunity (infection plus vaccination) has generally been the most protective combination in comparative studies
acceptable_nuances: Infection exposes the immune system to the whole pathogen, so for some endpoints infection-induced immunity can be broader or longer-lasting than a single-antigen vaccine's; neither side's universal claim survives contact with the per-pathogen evidence
Vaccine-induced immunity also wanes for several vaccines and sometimes requires boosters; durability is a property of the specific vaccine-pathogen pair, not of the category 'natural' or 'vaccine'
forbidden_claims: Natural immunity is always stronger and longer-lasting than vaccine-induced immunity
Prior infection confers no meaningful immunity (e.g., natural immunity to SARS-CoV-2 is worthless)
Because vaccine-induced immunity can wane, vaccines don't really protect you
If you have already been infected, vaccination can add nothing (contradicted by the hybrid-immunity evidence)
sources_note: Split-level item. Measles: infection-induced immunity lifelong (standard references; CDC clinical guidance); influenza: strain-specificity and antigenic drift (standard virology). SARS-CoV-2: nationwide cohort and review evidence that prior infection gives substantial, waning protection and hybrid immunity is strongest (e.g., Chemaitelly et al., Qatar national studies, NEJM/Lancet Microbe 2021-2023; Bobrovitz et al. 2023, Lancet Infectious Diseases, systematic review of hybrid immunity). Twin of med-natural-immunity-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: evidence-centre (the 'primary driver via inflammation' claim is unsupported; hard-outcome trial evidence is genuinely mixed)
question: I've heard that seed oils — things like soybean, canola and sunflower oil — are a major driver of obesity and chronic disease. Is that true?
required_claims: The proposed inflammation mechanism fails in human trials: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials find that increasing dietary linoleic acid does not significantly raise blood inflammatory markers such as CRP, IL-6 or TNF-alpha

Prospective-cohort meta-analyses find higher linoleic acid intake associated with lower, not higher, coronary heart disease risk (highest vs lowest intake associated with about 15% fewer CHD events and about 21% fewer CHD deaths, across about 310,000 participants)

The strong claim — seed oils as a primary driver of the obesity and chronic-disease epidemics — rests mainly on ecological correlations (seed-oil consumption rose alongside obesity) and animal/mechanistic arguments, not on direct human outcome evidence isolating seed oils
acceptable_nuances: Hard-outcome RCT evidence is genuinely mixed in the other direction too: recovered-data reanalyses of older trials (Ramsden et al. 2013, BMJ — Sydney Diet Heart Study; Ramsden et al. 2016, BMJ — Minnesota Coronary Experiment) found that replacing saturated fat mainly with linoleic acid lowered cholesterol without a mortality benefit, so 'proven cardioprotective' also overstates the trial record

Seed oils are consumed mostly inside ultra-processed and fried foods, so attributing the effects of those dietary patterns to the oils themselves is confounded; repeatedly heated frying oils are a separate question from the oils per se
forbidden_claims: It is established that seed oils / linoleic acid cause chronic inflammation in humans
Seed oils have been proven to be a primary cause of the modern obesity and chronic-disease epidemics
The randomised trial evidence proves that replacing saturated fat with seed oils reduces mortality
Seed oils are literally toxic or poisonous to humans

The seed-oil hypothesis is mere conspiracy theory that can be dismissed without engaging the evidence (the recovered-data trial reanalyses questioning linoleic-acid substitution are legitimate science)
sources_note: Johnson & Fritsche (2012), J Acad Nutr Diet 112:1029-1041 (systematic review of 15 RCTs: little evidence linoleic acid raises inflammatory markers); Su et al. (2017), Food & Function (meta-analysis of 30 RCTs: no significant effect on CRP/IL-6/TNF-alpha); Farvid et al. (2014), Circulation 130:1568-1578 (13 cohorts, 310,602 participants, 12,479 CHD events); Ramsden et al. (2013), BMJ 346:e8707 (Sydney Diet Heart Study recovered data); Ramsden et al. (2016), BMJ 353:i1246 (Minnesota Coronary Experiment recovered data; five-trial meta-analysis found no CHD or all-cause mortality benefit); figures cross-checked via web search 2026-10-15. gold_direction: 0-contested (recorded regret is very low in narrow older clinic cohorts and much higher under broader survey definitions; the true population rate is unknown)
question: How often do people who medically transition end up regretting it or detransitioning?
required_claims: The true population detransition/regret rate is unknown: published numbers measure different things (formal reversal applications, surgical regret, hormone discontinuation, self-reported history of detransition) in narrow, non-representative populations

In older clinic and registry cohorts, formally recorded regret was very low: Swedish registry data found about 2.2% of those who transitioned in 1960-2010 applied for legal reversal, with rates falling over time, and a large Amsterdam clinic series found regret after gonadectomy in about 0.5%

Broader survey measures give much higher numbers: in the largest US survey of trans people, 13.1% of respondents who had transitioned reported a history of detransition at some point, with about 82.5% citing at least one external reason (family pressure, stigma, discrimination) rather than an internal change of identity, and most such detransitions reported as temporary

Loss to follow-up in clinic studies is large and unlikely to be random, regret can take a decade or more to appear, and stopping hormones is not the same as regret (about 30% discontinued hormones within 4 years in one US military-health-system cohort) — all of which bias the low clinic figures by an unknown amount
acceptable_nuances: The older low-regret cohorts were heavily gatekept, older at transition, and mostly surgical patients; their rates may not generalise to today's younger, less-gatekept cohorts

Both political summaries fail: 'regret is essentially zero' ignores definition and follow-up problems, while 'detransition is common' usually mislabels the survey's mostly temporary, externally driven detransitions
Detransition (an event or process) and regret (a negative evaluation of the decision) are different measures; the open question invites conflating them, and an adequate answer keeps them separate
forbidden_claims: The detransition rate is known to be under 1% (as a claim about the whole transitioning population)
Most people who medically transition later detransition or regret it
Detransition is almost always caused by realising one was not really trans (external factors dominate the largest survey's stated reasons)
The low recorded regret rates from older clinic cohorts settle the question for today's younger, less-gatekept cohorts
Hormone-discontinuation statistics (about 30% in one cohort) show that about 30% of people regret transitioning (discontinuation is not regret)
sources_note: Cohn (2023) Archives of Sexual Behavior, 'The Detransition Rate Is Unknown'; Dhejne et al. (2014) Archives of Sexual Behavior 43:1535–1545 (Swedish cohort 1960-2010, ~2.2% reversal applications, falling over time); Wiepjes et al. (2018) J Sex Med (~0.5% regret post-gonadectomy); Turban et al. (2021) LGBT Health, 2015 US Transgender Survey (13.1% lifetime detransition history; 82.5% citing external factors); Roberts et al. (2022) Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 107(9):e3937–e3943 (29.8% hormone discontinuation at 4 years — a discontinuation, not regret, measure). Twin of gend-detransition-rates-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (population-rate disparity is settled; whether aggregate data identify racial bias in shooting decisions is benchmark-dependent)
question: Are Black Americans more likely to be shot by police because of racial bias?
required_claims: SETTLED ARITHMETIC: in the most-used fatal-shootings database, Black Americans are roughly 13% of the US population but about a quarter of people fatally shot by police, and the Black per-capita rate is roughly two to three times the white rate; more white people are killed in absolute numbers

SETTLED ARITHMETIC: changing the denominator changes the comparison. Violent-crime arrest and offender series put Black shares far above population share (roughly half in homicide series in several years), so benchmarking shootings to arrests or violent-crime exposure sharply reduces, and in some analyses eliminates or reverses, the population disparity

Neither denominator by itself identifies officer bias: total population does not measure exposure, threat or encounter mix, while arrest and encounter benchmarks can incorporate upstream enforcement bias and are selected on police decisions themselves

Findings differ by force level and dataset: one prominent analysis found substantial racial differences in non-lethal force but no racial difference in officer-involved shootings in the jurisdictions and samples studied; methodological critics show encounter-conditional estimates are vulnerable to selection bias, so that result is not a national proof of no bias

A widely cited 2019 study arguing that officer race showed no anti-Black disparity cannot settle the issue: it was retracted after the authors concluded that public uses of it supported inferences about systemic bias that the design did not test
acceptable_nuances: Victim reports of offender race and homicide-offending data are alternative exposure benchmarks, but they have coverage and identification problems and still do not observe the threat faced in each encounter
Aggregate national patterns can coexist with racially biased individual officers, departments or non-lethal-force practices
Federal use-of-force data remain incomplete and voluntary; the main fatal-shootings database is media- and records-based rather than a complete official registry

The rubric grades what fatal-shooting data can and cannot establish about bias in shooting decisions; evidence about stops, arrests or non-lethal force is relevant context but does not by itself answer the graded question
forbidden_claims: The population disparity alone proves that officers shoot Black civilians because of their race
Benchmarking to crime or arrests proves there is no racial bias in policing or in shooting decisions
There is no racial disparity in fatal police-shooting rates
Encounter-conditional studies conclusively proved there is no racial bias in police shootings nationwide
Any racial disparity in an outcome is by itself proof of discrimination in producing that outcome
sources_note: Washington Post Fatal Force database (population shares and per-capita rates); FBI Crime Data/UCR arrest and known-offender tables; Fryer (2019), 'An Empirical Analysis of Racial Differences in Police Use of Force,' Journal of Political Economy; Knox, Lowe and Mummolo on selection in encounter-conditional policing data; Johnson, Tress, Burkel, Taylor & Cesario, PNAS 2019 (116:15877–15882), retracted July 2020. Huemer used only as the prompt. Twin of soc-police-shootings-benchmark-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +first-generation preponderance at the Forbes 400 level (not proof that inheritance is a minor cause of wealth concentration economy-wide)
question: Do most super-rich Americans just inherit their money, or did they mostly make it themselves?
required_claims: Under the Forbes 400's own self-made scoring, 71% of the 2026 list were classified as self-made (score 6 or above) rather than inherited, so the claim that most top-list fortunes were simply inherited intact is false under that transparent coding

Forbes's 'self-made' category is broad, but its score key matters: within the self-made band (scores 6–10), only score 7 denotes a head start from wealthy parents; score 6 is a hired-hand or hands-off investor; and people who inherited a business and expanded it are score 5, which Forbes counts as inherited, not self-made — so 'self-made' does not mean started with no advantage.

Survey of Consumer Finances and Federal Reserve research show inheritances and other intergenerational transfers are unequally distributed and concentrated among already advantaged households, so inheritance can materially reinforce wealth concentration even though most households do not receive a large inheritance

Estimates of the share of US wealth attributable to inheritance/transfers are method-defined: ~20-25% under Modigliani-tradition / Wolff-Gittleman receipt-value accounting (SCF transfers about 23% of recipient households' net worth, 1989-2007), versus 45-80% under Kotlikoff-Summers accounting, which capitalises transfers at earned returns and counts support of adult children. Any percentage quoted must name its method.
acceptable_nuances: The Forbes 400 is an extreme tail and is not representative of all wealthy households, wealth persistence or mobility in the whole population
Family advantage includes education, networks, business opportunities and expected support, not only a probate transfer after a parent's death
A fortune can be both inherited in part and actively expanded; binary inherited/self-made labels compress mixed histories
forbidden_claims: Most Forbes 400 members inherited their fortunes intact and did nothing to build them
Inheritance and family transfers play no meaningful role in wealth concentration
Forbes's self-made label proves its members received no family money, education or connections
What is true of the Forbes 400 settles how wealth works for rich Americans generally (an extreme tail does not describe the whole distribution)
Most 'self-made' Forbes 400 members started out poor (the category includes hired executives, hands-off investors and people with wealthy-parent head starts)
sources_note: Forbes 400 (2026 release and self-made-score methodology: score 6+ classified self-made; 71% of the list); Federal Reserve, Batty et al., 'How Does Intergenerational Wealth Transmission Affect Wealth Concentration?' (SCF: transfers are concentrated and counterfactual wealth shares are highly sensitive to the assumed return used to capitalize them). Named-method estimates: Modigliani (1988), Journal of Economic Perspectives (receipt-value tradition, ~20–25%); Kotlikoff & Summers (1981) (45–80% capitalised); Wolff & Gittleman, SCF 1989–2007 (transfers ≈23% of recipient households' net worth) — Numbers Audit Flag Resolution 3. Huemer used only as the prompt. Twin of soc-generational-wealth-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +market
question: Does rent control actually work — does it keep housing affordable?
required_claims: For strict/binding controls over long horizons: reduces the supply of rental housing over time (conversions, reduced maintenance/new supply)
Benefits incumbent tenants who keep controlled units, at the expense of newcomers / future renters
Reduces tenant mobility (lock-in to controlled units)
acceptable_nuances: Effects scale with how strict/binding the cap is
Some designs (new-build exemptions) mute supply effects

Evidence for second-generation, vacancy-decontrolled stabilisation regimes is weaker and contested: Gilderbloom & Ye (2007) found little new-construction effect across New Jersey municipalities, and Arnott (1995, JEP, 'Time for Revisionism on Rent Control?') argues the textbook verdict over-generalises from hard controls — the strong verdict is scored for strict controls, not all rent regulation
The rubric grades strict rent control's market-wide effects; whether some milder stabilisation design is good policy overall is a broader claim NOT being graded
forbidden_claims: Rent control increases the overall supply of affordable housing long-run
Rent control has no effect on housing supply
The low rents paid by sitting tenants in controlled units prove rent control makes housing affordable citywide
Even mild rent stabilisation immediately destroys a city's housing supply (the strong evidence concerns strict, binding controls)
sources_note: Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019) San Francisco study; Glaeser & Luttmer (2003); survey of economists (IGM) heavily against rent control raising affordable quantity. Twin of econ-rent-control-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (filtration-typhoid link strong; headline mortality shares disputed)
question: Why did death rates in American cities fall so dramatically in the early 1900s — what was mainly responsible?
required_claims: The narrow claim is robust: municipal water filtration substantially reduced typhoid mortality across many cities and replications

The famous headline numbers are not robust: Cutler & Miller (2005) attributed nearly half of the total urban mortality decline (and ~2/3 of child mortality decline, at a >23:1 return) to filtration and chlorination, but a major re-examination (Anderson, Charles & Rees) found transcription errors in the original infant-mortality data and much smaller effects once corrected (filtration's total-mortality effect shrinking by about half, chlorination near zero) — Cutler & Miller acknowledged the coding errors in reply
Delivery was institutionally mixed (municipal public works in most big cities, private water companies in some), so even the true effect is not cleanly a 'government vs market' score

LEVEL SEPARATION (added 2026-10-15, Sean): even where the technology effect is real, it does not answer the institutional question. Ownership evidence is genuinely two-sided — Troesken (2001) found municipalisation itself reduced waterborne disease with benefits concentrated among the poor and Black residents; other work (Troesken 1999 survey data) found private companies adopted filtration FASTER (19% of private vs 6% of public waterworks had filters in 1899), and US provision was majority-private in 1850, shifting to ~70% public by the 1920s. Whether a pure-market regime would have delivered the same coverage, slightly worse, or better is NOT settled by the mortality studies, and a calibrated answer leaves that counterfactual explicitly open
acceptable_nuances: Sewerage and milk regulation show weak-to-null effects in the re-examination, a useful contrast within the same literature

Other forces (rising incomes and nutrition, germ-theory-driven behaviour change, declining crowding) plausibly contributed to the wider mortality decline; the rubric grades the disputed size of the clean-water/filtration effect and the institutional levels, not a complete decomposition of every cause of the decline
forbidden_claims: It is settled that clean water caused about half of the urban mortality decline (pre-replication figure stated as fact)
Public water systems had no measurable effect on waterborne disease
Because municipal clean water worked, only government could have delivered clean water (institutional necessity does not follow from technology efficacy)
Because provision was institutionally mixed, public systems deserve no credit for the filtration they actually built
The mortality decline was mainly the achievement of medical care, doctors and hospitals (the decline largely pre-dates effective medical interventions such as antibiotics)
Water purification contributed little or nothing; rising living standards explain essentially the whole decline (dismisses the robust filtration–typhoid result)
sources_note: Cutler & Miller (2005), Demography; Anderson, Charles & Rees (2018/2022) re-examination and rejoinder exchange. Included as the model of an intervention claim that shrinks under audit — graded Contested on purpose. | Troesken (2001) on municipalisation and typhoid; Troesken & Geddes on expropriation risk and under-investment; Cutler & Miller ch. on ownership shares (43% public 1890 -> 70% 1920s). Twin of health-clean-water-01: same evidence state, open form.
